newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - HK memorabilia challenge taste barriers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK memorabilia challenge taste barriers.

text.p: Souvenir seekers with a yen for the tacky, the trendy or the timeless -- Hong Kong has something for everyone as it prepares to rejoin China.
Hong Kong merchants seldom have found anything too ugly or useless to sell in this ultra-capitalist bastion.
The transition to communist-ruled China has unleashed a stream of "1997" keepsakes, including predictable T-shirts, mugs and plaques. Other items are bizarre in taste and design.
GOOEY DRAGONS AND PINK DOLPHINS
"Tacky" is the word for one memento on offer, a wobbly, finger-sized soft rubber "Lucky Dragon" that retails for HK$19.97 (US$2.60).

"The Chinese regard themselves as children of the dragon, so this signifies the new Hong Kong that is going to come about," said C.P. Ho, chairman and chief executive at Eye On Ltd, which developed the dragon.
The gooey puppet proudly waves the five-star flag of China and Hong Kong's own banner featuring the bauhinia flower that is the territory's acutely apolitical symbol.
The grinning dragon, which comes in seven flashy colours, also sports a rendering of the Hong Kong skyline on its belly.
Fold the creature up into an "egg" and it will "magically come out of its pouch in a thousand and one ways".

A cuter alternative is the pink dolphin, the endangered Pearl River dweller chosen as the 1997 mascot by the Association for the Reunification of Hong Kong with China, the group coordinating the official celebrations.
Fewer than 200 of the bubble-gum pink porpoises can be seen in the wild but thousands will be visible on T-shirts and coffee mugs and in the form of cuddly, plush toys.
ARROGANCE GETS THE CAN AS BRITISH LEAVE
Britain will give up its last colony in the Far East at midnight on June 30 when it returns Hong Kong to China after more than 150 years of rule.
American entrepreneurs, quick to see a Hong Kong buck, are offering "canned colonial air" to those nostalgic for the British empire.
The label of the "100 percent pure pomposity" product warns that "one sniff leads to extreme arrogance".

Afraid your friends won't believe you were here? The Hong Kong Tourist Association offers a document certifying the bearer "was in Hong Kong to witness the historic change in sovereignty in 1997" as one of its new handover keepsakes.
For those who don't like their memories to last too long, there are Hong Kong cigarettes, candy and an official 1997 wine. Other keepsakes are unlikely to be throwaways.
BAUHINIA BAUBLES AND EMPRESS BARBIE

The well-dressed woman can own Special Administrative Region jewellery in the form of bauhinia flower finery. Gold and silver versions sell for the same price, HK$750 for the brooch and HK$600 for the pendant.
She can also buy a Chinese Last Empress Barbie doll (with black hair, not blonde) for her daughter, or keep it for herself for HK$540.
And, why preserve your handover memories on film when you can preserve them on the camera?
For a mere HK$68,000, photo buffs can buy a limited-edition titanium Leica camera engraved with famous Hong Kong buildings on its dome and a gold plate celebrating the handover on its back.
The truly sentimental can get a Baccarat crystal sculpture of a mother and child, symbolising the powerful bond between China and Hong Kong. The price? HK$338,000.
Hong Kong being Hong Kong, many of the most popular souvenirs offer the possibility of profit.

Thousands of Hong Kong stamp fanciers queued up for hours earlier this year to buy special handover stamps, many in the hope the sticky symbols of empire will some day be worth far more than the few Hong Kong dollars they cost in 1997.

The post office now sells its special issues over the course of days rather than hours following the death in March of a 71-year-old philatelist who suffered a heart attack in the stampede to buy the last stamps bearing Queen Elizabeth's head.
